title: How the Space Race Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the Space Race, the Cold War competition between the United States and the Soviet Union to dominate spaceflight. They trace its roots to German rocket scientists such as Wernher von Braun, who were brought to the US and the USSR after World War II (Sergei Korolev led the Soviet effort). They cover early milestones: Sputnik (October 4, 1957), Explorer 1 (January 31, 1958), Project Mercury, Yuri Gagarin's orbit (April 12, 1961), Kennedy's moon pledge, Gemini, Apollo 1's fire, and the Apollo-Soyuz docking (1975). They also discuss the differences between the two programs, the Apollo 11 landing, later cooperation leading to the International Space Station, the uncertain future of US human spaceflight, China's program, a list of space myths and inventions (Velcro, the space pen, Tang), and a listener letter about breastfeeding.

segments.title: Opening banter and Apollo 11 recollections
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the show's opening false start and reminisce about the space program. They mention space museums and Space Camp, plan future episodes on the Moon landing and space stations, and recall The Right Stuff. They also discuss the tense final seconds of the Apollo 11 landing.

segments.title: Defining the Space Race
segments.summary: The hosts define the Space Race as a Cold War byproduct of US-Soviet rivalry. They describe how each side pushed the other to advance technologically, and how early programs proceeded in logical steps.

segments.title: German rocket scientists and the V-2
segments.summary: The hosts describe Wernher von Braun and the V-2 rocket. They explain that von Braun and colleagues surrendered to the Americans, who brought them to White Sands, New Mexico. The Soviets similarly recruited Nazi rocket scientists, and Sergei Korolev led their program.

segments.title: Early satellites and the International Geophysical Year
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Eisenhower's national security space programs, including the reconnaissance program Corona, and the International Geophysical Year. Both nations decided to launch satellites, which started the race.

segments.title: Sputnik, Explorer 1 and the start of NASA
segments.summary: The Soviets launched Sputnik on October 4, 1957, and the US launched Explorer 1 on January 31, 1958, on a Juno rocket designed by von Braun. The hosts say the US could have launched earlier with von Braun's design. Congress then passed the Space Act, creating NASA, and the Soviets set up their own program.

segments.title: Mercury, Vostok and differences between the programs
segments.summary: The hosts compare the American Mercury program, which used Redstone and Atlas rockets and pilots who splashed down in the ocean, with the Soviet Vostok program. The Soviets kept their program secret and used spherical capsules that landed on land. The hosts also discuss the origin of the word cosmonaut.

segments.title: Failures, Gagarin and Kennedy's moon pledge
segments.summary: The hosts describe early failed launches and the Apollo 1 test fire that killed three astronauts. They then cover Yuri Gagarin's orbit on April 12, 1961, and Valentina Tereshkova's 48 orbits. Kennedy then pledged a Moon landing before the decade was out.

segments.title: Gemini, Apollo 1 and later Soviet and American programs
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Gemini program, which showed rendezvous and docking and long stays in orbit. They then cover the Apollo 1 fire, the Soviets' shift toward unmanned missions and space stations, and the Apollo-Soyuz docking of 1975.
